name: VEXpath
one_liner: Self-hostable VEX decision engine for embedded device makers: turns Yocto build data, vendor CSAF and Dependency-Track findings into signed, evidence-backed per-release VEX.
entry_price: EUR 290/month billed annually (EUR 3,480/year) for up to 5 product lines, self-hosted; EUR 49 per additional product line per month with no tier cap; EU single-tenant hosting +EUR 150/month
fatal: Most dangerous competitor: Bootlin's sbom-cve-check. It has been the Yocto Project's official CVE-monitoring tool since the Wrynose release, it is free (GPLv2), and it works on exactly the inputs VEXpath reads: the SPDX3 SBOM and the vex.bbclass rootfs.json. It marks kernel CVEs not applicable when the affected source file is not compiled in, which is finer than VEXpath's kernel-option rule. It also exports a Yocto VEX manifest with statements and justifications and emits not_affected for disputed CVEs. This is the 'paid additional cut' in the wedge, and every Yocto user now gets it upstream for free.
majors: market-skeptic

The repositioned compliance hook does not carry the product. Art. 14(8) requires informing users, 'where appropriate' in machine-readable form, only after the manufacturer becomes aware of an actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident. That is a rare event for a mid-size maker and is a notification duty, not a duty to publish per-release not_affected VEX across all findings. The bulk of VEXpath's value (noise cut, cross-release ledger) has no regulatory pull; it relies on OEM customer demand that the evidence does not show.
market-skeptic

Demand evidence is unchanged: developer GitHub issues (engagement 1-43), some from open-source maintainers with no budget, and none from a Yocto device maker's PSIRT or CRA owner. The revision admits this in risks and moves the burden to the riskiest-assumption test, which is right, but until that test runs there is no sign of budgeted pain in the named segment.
market-skeptic

The narrowing compounds the size problem. The buyer now has to be an EU maker with 50-1,000 staff, firmware on Yocto/embedded Linux, already producing SBOMs, already running Dependency-Track or OE cve-check, and with a named CRA owner. Each filter cuts the pool; the concept itself guesses 'a few thousand' for a broader profile with no source. At EUR 3.5k ACV, even 300 customers is about EUR 1M ARR, so the segment may not support a venture-scale company.
market-skeptic

Budget competition inside the CRA stack. CVD Portal sells Art. 14 reporting plus SBOM management, remediation tracking and CSAF advisories from EUR 1,188-3,588/yr, grant-eligible. VEXpath at EUR 3,480/yr roughly doubles a mid-size maker's CRA tooling spend for one sub-step that the suite already lists. Buyers who must justify spend to a regulatory or quality manager will likely accept the suite's manual VEX first.
competitor-analyst

Lynx (Timesys) Vigiles is an established commercial product for this exact buyer, and the concept leaves it out. Its meta-timesys Yocto layer uploads the kernel and U-Boot .config to filter CVEs and keeps a not-affected list. It markets triage decisions, release-by-release records of how each CVE was handled, VEX export, KEV prioritisation and EU CRA reporting for embedded Linux, Yocto, Buildroot and custom BSPs. It also has NXP as a BSP distribution channel. VEXpath's line that 'nobody affordable turns embedded build evidence into reviewed VEX' is not supported until it is checked against Vigiles' pricing and NXP bundle.
competitor-analyst

Free open-source tools already cover the rest of the embedded workbench. bitvex is a free CLI that turns Yocto SPDX into OpenVEX using kernel .config, device-tree 'disabled' peripherals and U-Boot config. It also produces delta VEX between builds and has a watch mode that re-scans when SBOMs or configs change, which is close to VEXpath's invalidation idea. VulnScout from Savoir-faire Linux imports Yocto cve-check/VEX with SPDX, has a triage UI, records VEX assessments with AI suggestions that need human approval, and exports CycloneDX and OpenVEX. Device-tree filtering already goes further than VEXpath's MVP.
competitor-analyst

What remains distinct is two-way Dependency-Track sync, invalidation of inherited decisions and signing with the customer's key. These are workflow features, not a product moat. Any of the above could add them, and so could DT 5.1, since its VEX import already exists. sbom-cve-check output plus DT VEX import already gets most teams the free importer that VEXpath plans to give away.
security-practitioner

The kernel-config evidence rule is already in free upstream tooling. OE-core's improve_kernel_cve_report.py takes the compiled-file list from the kernel SPDX and marks a version-affected CVE as 'not-applicable-config' when its programFiles were not compiled. Kernel CVEs are the bulk of embedded Linux noise. Teams on current Yocto who run this plus vex.bbclass will import an already-reduced report into DT. The 'additional cut' shown in the wedge may be small, and that is exactly the number the buyer's engineer will check.
security-practitioner

Workflow competition from a free Yocto-native triage UI. Savoir-faire Linux's VulnScout (GPL-3.0) ingests Yocto cve-check/VEX, SPDX and CycloneDX, has a web triage UI with VEX assessments per project and variant, CI policy checks and CycloneDX/OpenVEX export. Embedded teams evaluating 'a triage tool beside our build' will find it first. VEXpath's remaining edge for a practitioner is DT write-back, cross-release invalidation, CSAF export and signing. Those are real but narrower, and the concept does not list VulnScout.
security-practitioner

The invalidation rule fights reuse. A new firmware release almost always changes some component versions and the image's build-config hash. If any change to 'build-config hash' re-opens an inherited decision, most decisions re-open every release and the cross-release time saving disappears. If the rule is scoped per component (the relevant recipe's config and patches, or the kernel options touched by the CVE's files), it must be shown to be safe. The design needs per-finding evidence fingerprints, not a global hash. As written, the rule is either unsafe or unhelpful.
technical-feasibility

The core build-evidence join is harder than the feature list implies. vex.bbclass writes per-recipe status keyed by recipe name and CVE_PRODUCT (an NVD/CPE product name), with no PURLs. Dependency-Track findings are keyed by the SBOM component's PURL/CPE. Where the SBOM came from Syft/Trivy scanning a rootfs rather than Yocto's own SPDX, recipe-to-component mapping is fuzzy, and a wrong match can wrongly carry a not_affected status. v1 should require a Yocto-generated SBOM, or treat unmatched components as a hard 'no evidence' result.
technical-feasibility

Coverage across Yocto releases. vex.bbclass and OE's kernel CVE enrichment script are on scarthgap but not on kirkstone. Kirkstone is still common in vendor BSPs (NXP, TI and others lag), so the ingest must also parse older cve-check JSON and handle per-branch format differences. That adds to an already tight six months and to every later release.
gtm-pricing

The free baseline moved up under the price. Yocto 6.0 made Bootlin's sbom-cve-check the official CVE tool. It consumes vex.bbclass CVE_STATUS and OpenVEX annotations and treats CVEs in sources that are not compiled in as not applicable. OE-Core's improve_kernel_cve_report.py does the same for kernel CVEs using compiled-file lists. Two of VEXpath's core evidence rules (CVE_STATUS, kernel 'code not present') are therefore free in the buyer's build. EUR 290/month has to be justified by the ledger, invalidation, DT write-back and signing alone. The riskiest-assumption test measures the cut against 'DT 5.1 + CVE_STATUS', not against sbom-cve-check, so it overstates the value buyers will pay for.
gtm-pricing

The revenue ceiling is too low for the team. The segment is 'a few thousand' EU embedded-Linux makers (concept:open_questions[4]). A product-led funnel from a niche open-source importer that converts 1-3% gives tens of customers at about EUR 3.5-8k each, roughly EUR 100-300k ARR after 18-24 months. That does not fund 3 FTEs plus self-hosted support. Partner resale margins (typically 20-30%) cut net ACV further. The model needs either a much larger segment (software vendors, non-Yocto RTOS) or a higher price backed by proven time savings.
gtm-pricing

Self-hosted software bought by card is an unusual purchase path for 50-1,000-person industrial makers. On-prem software that touches unreleased firmware SBOMs normally goes through IT/security review, a supplier onboarding form and a PO. So the product-led motion may still stall in procurement, which revives the round-1 CAC problem. Self-hosting also brings per-customer support costs (upgrades, offline vulnerability feeds, DT version drift) that a EUR 3.5k ACV cannot absorb.
legal-ethics

VEXpath is itself a commercial product with digital elements sold in the EU, so the CRA applies to it. Its reporting duties under Art. 14 have applied since 11 Sep 2026. By 11 Dec 2027 it needs Annex I conformity, its own SBOM, a coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy, support-period commitments and CE marking. It is not an Annex III important product, so self-assessment is enough. Even so, the 6-month, two-engineer plan doesn't cost any of this in. A CRA tool that can't show its own compliance would hurt its credibility.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: On real Yocto/embedded-Linux firmware SBOMs, evidence rules resolve a large share of the findings that Dependency-Track 5.1 plus OpenEmbedded's own CVE_STATUS leave open, without wrong not_affected calls, and that saving is worth EUR 290/month to mid-size device makers.
riskiest_assumption.test: In 2 weeks, without building the product: (a) from 15 discovery calls with CRA owners at 50-500-person EU device makers (sourced via Yocto/OE and Dependency-Track communities and a CRA consultancy), collect 5 firmware SBOM + build-artefact sets under NDA, processed on the prospect's premises or an isolated laptop; apply the rules by hand with scripts and have the prospect's engineer review every not_affected; (b) at the end of each call show the result or a mock and ask for a paid design-partner LOI at the entry price.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: In at least 3 of 5 data sets, 30%+ of findings left open after DT 5.1 + CVE_STATUS are resolved with documented evidence and zero wrong not_affected on review; and at least 4 of 15 sign a LOI at EUR 290/month or more, with at least 3 accepting self-hosted deployment and naming who approves the spend.

change_my_mind: market-skeptic
At least 4 of 15 CRA owners at 50-500-person EU Yocto device makers sign a EUR 290/month LOI with a named spend approver (the concept's own test).
competitor-analyst

A side-by-side test on 3 real Yocto firmware data sets showing VEXpath resolves 30%+ more findings, with zero wrong not_affected calls, than sbom-cve-check (compiled-sources on) plus bitvex, after both are imported into DT 5.1.
security-practitioner

On 5 real Yocto firmware data sets, after vex.bbclass, improve_kernel_cve_report.py with SPDX compiled files, and DT 5.1, VEXpath resolves 30%+ of the remaining findings with zero wrong not_affected on engineer review.
technical-feasibility
A prototype that joins vex.bbclass/cve-check output to DT findings on 3 real firmware builds (at least one kirkstone), with match coverage reported and zero wrong carries on manual review.
gtm-pricing
On 5 prospect data sets, VEXpath resolves 30%+ of findings that remain open after Yocto 6.0 sbom-cve-check (with compiled-source filtering) plus DT 5.1, with zero wrong not_affected.
legal-ethics

A dated plan, with a budget, for VEXpath's own CRA compliance: a published CVD policy and security contact, a product SBOM, the Art. 14 reporting process, a stated support period, and Annex I self-assessment before Dec 2027.

name: LeaverCheck
one_liner: Read-only offboarding verification: within an hour of an Okta or Entra deactivation, checks every app, including non-SCIM ones, and chases leftover accounts.
entry_price: $1/user/month billed annually (minimum $250/month), unlimited apps; free one-time orphan-account scan from CSV exports
fatal: Most dangerous competitor: Vanta, with Drata close behind. The buyer is defined by a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 cycle, so most already pay for one of them. Vanta starts offboarding when the IdP suspends a user (or the HRIS marks them terminated). It lists the leaver's known accounts, auto-detects deactivation in monitored integrations, assigns tasks for the rest, and blocks completion until those are done. Drata's tests fail when a terminated person keeps access in connected systems, under a one-business-day control. LeaverCheck's per-leaver check, chase-up and auditor log largely duplicate a tool the buyer already owns, and the concept's competitor table omits both.
majors: market-skeptic

Verification-only is a vitamin on top of a painkiller the buyer already has. The buyer keeps paying for whatever path does the deprovisioning (LCM, Scimify, Workflows, tickets) and is asked to add a budget line to check it. The concept admits auditors accept ticketed offboarding and that buyers must 'value catching misses sooner, not just passing the audit'. No budget exists for that today.
market-skeptic

Still no evidence from the named buyer. The revision says so ('the input has no more buyer-side evidence'). Need statements remain developers asking for SCIM in their own products, plus one HN comment. WTP is still 2 of 5. Every demand claim now rests on a test that has not run.
market-skeptic

The incidence data that would show the pain is common comes from vendors and skews to enterprise. CloudEagle's '48% of former employees still have active access' comes from a survey of 1,000 enterprise CIOs/CISOs by a vendor selling the fix, not from 150-1,500-person companies. Leftover accounts in SSO-enforced apps can't be logged into once the IdP account is deactivated, so the urgent pain is limited to apps that use local logins. That is a smaller set than '10+ non-SCIM apps'.
market-skeptic

The revenue ceiling looks small. At $1/user/month with a $250 minimum, ACV is about $3K-18K and typically about $6K. Suppose roughly 10-20K reachable US and EU tech or services firms of 150-1,500 employees run Okta or Entra with SOC 2 (my estimate). Then 2% penetration is about 300 customers, or about $2M ARR. That supports a small business but needs near-zero CAC, which founder-led sales does not provide.
competitor-analyst

The remaining wedge, apps with no integration, is a short step for the incumbents. Vanta already has a private-integration API that pushes user accounts in and links them to IdP users for account tests, an Access File Uploader for apps it can't connect to, and an offboarding API. Adding 'upload this app's export, diff it against leavers' to offboarding is a feature, not a product, and could ship next quarter. Meanwhile the GTM plans to partner with these same compliance-automation tools, which hands the most likely acquirer-or-cloner the roadmap.
competitor-analyst

Nudge Security sells offboarding for exactly the 'beyond the IdP' gap, and is missing from the table. It discovers SaaS accounts, shadow IT and OAuth grants per identity, including apps outside SSO. It nudges IT or users to remove access where it can't automate. It uses password resets to lock leavers out of unmanaged accounts. It offers 'find lingering access on Day One' of a free trial, the same hook as LeaverCheck's free scan, but needs no CSVs from app owners.
competitor-analyst

SaaS-management and IGA platforms (Zluri, Torii, Lumos, Stitchflow, ConductorOne) already sell user-list reconciliation, and Okta ISPM covers identity posture. ConductorOne's Apache-2.0 Baton toolkit lists principals across apps and diffs sync runs, now continued in baton-sdk. That gives a scripting IT team, or any bridge vendor such as Scimify or Aquera, a free read-only connector base to build the same check.
security-practitioner

The trigger isn't reliable. Okta event hooks are best-effort, retry at most once, time out after 3 seconds and guarantee no maximum delay, so a dropped deactivation event means that leaver is never checked, with no visible error. Leavers who are suspended, unassigned from the app group, or disabled by HR-driven Entra sync (rather than deactivated) may not fire the expected event at all. Without a periodic reconciliation against the System Log, Entra audit logs and directory state, the per-leaver log misses exactly the cases it exists to catch.
security-practitioner

Export-fed apps get weak assurance. In the long tail, which is also where SSO usually isn't enforced and the real risk sits, the data the check relies on comes from the same app owner who is supposed to remove the account. That owner can upload a stale, filtered or edited CSV, and nothing proves the export is complete or recent. A 'checked' entry built on a three-week-old export looks the same in an audit log as a live API read unless the log records the data source, the export's timestamp and who uploaded it, and flags stale exports as not checked.
security-practitioner

Risk coverage is incomplete. A leaver is only truly gone when their personal API tokens, OAuth grants to third-party apps, active sessions, shared or service accounts they knew the password to, and SSH or deploy keys are also gone. A user-list check sees none of these. In SSO-enforced apps, which are the API-connected ones, the main residual risk is exactly these tokens, so a 'no leftover account' result can still leave live access. The pitch that leavers are 'actually gone everywhere' overstates what the product checks.
technical-feasibility

The trigger can't be relied on by itself. Okta event hooks are best-effort: delivery is at least once, Okta retries at most once, it doesn't retry 4xx responses, it times out after 3 seconds and it guarantees no maximum delay. A dropped hook means a leaver who is never checked, which gives silent false assurance. Entra has no equivalent push for audit events, so its checks depend on polling the audit log, and Entra Free keeps that log for only 7 days. The MVP needs a System Log and audit-log poller that reconciles against the hooks, idempotent handling of event IDs, and alerts when a poll falls behind.
technical-feasibility

Read-only list endpoints don't see everything, and some only come with admin-grade tokens. Notion's list-users excludes guests, so guest and contractor leftovers are invisible to it, and personal access tokens can't list users at all. Atlassian org API keys last at most a year, and without scopes they can reach every admin API. Slack needs users:read plus users:read.email to match on email. Each connector needs a documented coverage boundary (which account types, which plan tiers) shown per leaver, or the check log overstates what was checked.
gtm-pricing

The target buyer (a SOC 2/ISO shop with an audit in the next six months) very likely already pays for a compliance-automation platform. Vanta's offboarding workflow reportedly detects accounts in connected apps through mostly read-only integrations and auto-closes the task once deprovisioning is detected. Apps without an integration sit under 'Unmonitored Accounts', where an admin attests removal by hand. That covers most of LeaverCheck's value for API apps inside a budget line the buyer already has, so the channel plan to 'partner with compliance-automation tools' means courting the most dangerous substitute. What's left is better coverage of unmonitored apps, and that relies on CSV uploads, which is not much better than the attestation the buyer already does.
gtm-pricing

The price is set by a competitor anchor, not by value, and the anchor works against it. The rationale benchmarks Scimify at $0.90/user/month, but Scimify does the deprovisioning. Charging $1/user/month just to check is more than the bridge that does the work, which is a hard sentence for a buyer to accept. Per-IdP-user pricing also charges for every employee when the value sits in a handful of leavers a month on 10+ non-SCIM apps.
gtm-pricing

The unit economics are still thin. At $250/month minimum and about $6K for 500 users, a typical deal is $3-6K a year. The motion is founder-led sales opened by a concierge scan that someone diffs by hand, plus a GDPR DPA and a security review (lighter now, but still needed for holding the employee directory and read tokens). The concept rates willingness to pay 2 of 5. A $3-6K ACV can fund only self-serve conversion, and the funnel described is services-led.
legal-ethics

The riskiest-assumption test has 20 prospects send 90 days of IdP deactivations plus full user exports from 5-10 apps, diffed by hand in a spreadsheet, before the company has a DPA, sub-processor list, retention rule or SOC 2. That is personal data on employees and leavers, processed by a vendor that may not yet exist as a company. Under GDPR Art. 28 the controller may use only processors that give sufficient guarantees, under a contract. Many IT managers' own policies will stop them sharing this, and those who do share it create exposure for both sides.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: Mid-market IT teams on Okta or Entra find leftover accounts in non-SCIM apps often enough, and care enough, to pay about $1/user/month for continuous read-only leaver verification on top of whatever offboarding they already do.
riskiest_assumption.test: Over two weeks, offer 20 qualifying IT managers a free concierge orphan scan: they send the last 90 days of IdP deactivations plus user exports from 5-10 non-SCIM apps, and we diff them by hand in a spreadsheet. At the readout, ask for a paid pilot or LOI at $1/user/month.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: At least 8 of 20 scans find one or more active accounts belonging to a user deactivated in the IdP more than 7 days earlier, and at least 5 companies sign an LOI or paid pilot at $1/user/month or more.

change_my_mind: market-skeptic

The concierge test meets its own bar: at least 8 of 20 mid-market scans find active leftover accounts more than 7 days after IdP deactivation, at least half of them in apps without SSO enforcement, and at least 5 LOIs or paid pilots at $1/user/month or more.
competitor-analyst
At least 6 of the 20 concierge scans find leftover accounts at companies that already run Vanta or Drata offboarding, in apps those platforms mark as unmonitored or don't list.
security-practitioner
A daily reconciliation against the Okta System Log, Entra audit logs and directory state, which catches 100% of leavers in a pilot, including ones whose event hook delivery failed.
technical-feasibility
A per-app matrix for the 12 target connectors showing a non-admin list-users scope on the tiers buyers actually hold, plus which account types (guests, contractors, bots) each one misses
gtm-pricing
In the concierge test, at least 5 of 20 scanned companies already use Vanta or Drata and still find 1 or more active leaver accounts those tools missed
legal-ethics
A one-page DPA, NDA and 30-day deletion commitment signed before any concierge scan, with exports cut to identifier, status and role columns.

name: Keybridge
one_liner: Turns the static AWS and GCP keys your cross-cloud and GitHub Actions workloads still use into linted native-federation pull requests, run inside your cloud.
entry_price: Free self-hosted report; Migration $6,000 one-off per estate for up to 25 in-use boundary-crossing keys on the three supported paths ($150 per extra key); then Monitor $150/month flat for up to 100 AWS accounts and GCP projects.
majors: market-skeptic

Demand is still inferred. The revision keeps the same AWS-only developer issues, filed against upstream tools, and adds no buyer-side signal: no platform lead, auditor finding or consultancy describes in-use AWS-GCP or CI keys they would pay to remove. The concept admits this in risks[5] and riskiest_assumption.
market-skeptic

Narrowing the segment shrank the market without sizing it. The target is now AWS-primary and GCP-secondary companies with 50-1,000 employees that use GitHub Actions, have a GCP org created before 3 May 2024, have a CSPM key finding open for months, and run no Vault or Teleport. Each filter cuts the count, and no estimate is given. With about $7.8k of first-year value and mostly one-off revenue, $10M ARR needs roughly 1,300 new logos every year. That is implausible from an unsized niche.
market-skeptic

The problem is shrinking on the GCP half of the product. Datadog finds GCP service accounts with keys older than a year fell from 62% to 55% in a year. Google enforces key-creation blocking for every organisation created on or after 3 May 2024. Over half of old AWS keys are unused, which is hygiene and outside this product's scope. The pool of in-use, boundary-crossing keys may be only a handful per estate, and it gets smaller every year.
market-skeptic

The easiest share of the target keys, static AWS/GCP keys in GitHub Actions, already has official step-by-step guides and maintained actions. Teams that have left those findings open for months may be showing low priority rather than lack of capacity. If so, they will defer a $6,000 fee too, until an audit forces the work.
competitor-analyst

Most dangerous competitor is still Wiz, and its threat is no longer hypothetical. Wiz Code's Green Agent already does Keybridge's two paid steps for findings in general. It maps a cloud finding to its owner by correlating cloud logs, tags, commit history and service catalogs, then 'generates the exact code fix and opens a Pull Request', or passes the plan to a coding agent such as Claude Code. Wiz already sees in-use access keys across AWS and GCP in many target accounts. A key-to-federation fix is therefore a remediation template inside a shipping agent, not a new product. The concept still says Wiz 'stops at the finding'.
competitor-analyst

The IAM half of the paid migration is already free from an NHI vendor. Clutch Security publishes Federator under GPL-3.0, with Terraform templates for CI/CD-to-cloud federation (including GitHub Actions) and cloud-to-cloud IAM federation between AWS, Azure and GCP. These are Keybridge's three supported paths. Clutch's own process ends in a 'Protect' stage where static credentials are migrated to federation. The concept's Clutch row ('sold to enterprises; we do one narrow remediation job') misses that Clutch gives away the templates and owns the remediation story.
competitor-analyst

The consumer-side change is the new claimed moat (workflow YAML, Kubernetes annotation, credential-config file, removing env vars). Coding agents already produce exactly this kind of change, and Wiz now routes findings to them. Once a buyer has a key finding plus the free Federator templates and the cloud docs, Claude Code or Copilot can write the two-sided PR. The fixed $6,000 fee competes with an afternoon of agent-assisted work, not with five engineer-weeks. The concept's DIY anchor assumes manual work and is not evidenced.
security-practitioner

The PR path's permissions and hosting are not specified. The listed GitHub App scopes are org Secrets read and Contents read, and those cannot open PRs. Opening PRs needs Contents write and Pull requests write, and editing .github/workflows files needs the Workflows write permission. That last one lets the app change CI jobs that already hold cloud credentials. The concept doesn't say whether the App and its private key are hosted by the vendor or the customer. A vendor-hosted App with org-wide workflow write is exactly the custody the revision set out to remove. Security reviewers will ask for the App to be self-hosted or per-repo, or for PRs to be pushed from the customer's own runner.
security-practitioner

Attribution coverage will be partial for the most common consumers. CloudTrail management events record the access key ID, source IP and user agent. But S3 object reads and writes are data events and are not logged unless the customer enabled them, and many cross-cloud keys exist only to move data into or out of S3. On GCP, Data Access audit logs are off by default except for some BigQuery services, so GKE or Vertex consumers of JSON keys may show no data-plane trail. The 'unknown, no PR' rule is honest. It also means a sizable share of keys may get no remediation, and the share-attributed rate is the product's real efficacy number.
technical-feasibility

'AWS workload to GCP' counts as one path, but GCP documents three different mechanisms. The AWS provider and its credential config cover only EC2 VMs. EKS goes through the Kubernetes OIDC issuer setup with projected service-account tokens. Lambda and ECS need either env-var credentials or AWS outbound federation through a generic OIDC provider, plus an executable- or file-sourced credential config. The concept rules out shipping its own helper, but no maintained helper exists for that last case. So there are about five templates with their own consumer changes and test rigs, not three.
technical-feasibility

The access model doesn't match the feature. With only 'Secrets read' and 'Contents read', a GitHub App can't push a branch or open a PR. It also needs Contents write and Pull requests write on every consumer repo, and probably Workflows write, because the change edits .github/workflows files. Also, if Keybridge hosts the App, its private key and installation tokens sit with the vendor, which contradicts 'nothing leaves the customer's environment'. Each customer has to register their own App, or the tool has to run as an Action with a scoped token. That is install friction against the one-hour target.
technical-feasibility

Attribution still has blind spots that the confidence label hides rather than fixes. CloudTrail LookupEvents covers only management events for 90 days, one region per call, at 2 requests per second per account per region. A key used only for S3 Get/PutObject (the typical CI artifact upload) leaves no trace there. GitHub-hosted runners come from large shared IP ranges, so matching depends on secret names in workflows plus run timestamps. Expect a large 'unknown' share. That shrinks the set of keys you can sell a migration for, and it needs the customer to enable data-event trails first.
gtm-pricing

Revenue is mostly non-recurring. Year one is about $7,800 and year two is $1,800 (Monitor at $150/month), and the concept itself doubts that monitoring will be renewed. To reach $1M in new revenue a year, the company has to close about 130 migrations a year, each needing attribution review and merged PRs across repos it doesn't own. That is a productised-services business with a SaaS cost base (2 engineers plus SOC 2 Type I), not a recurring-revenue one. Nothing in the plan expands an account after the first migration.
gtm-pricing

The channel rests on two unproven bets. One is self-serve conversion of a $6k one-off buy, which still needs a GitHub App install with org Secrets read plus a security sign-off, so it is not a credit-card purchase. The other is consultancies reselling, which the concept itself lists as an open question because they may prefer to bill by the hour. With one founder-seller and both bets unproven, the motion defaults to founder-led selling, which the concept admits this ACV can't fund.
gtm-pricing

The DIY anchor is the vendor's own estimate and is weak at the expected estate size. The success signal expects a median of about 10 in-use keys. At 'one engineer-day per key' that is two engineer-weeks, so a $6,000 fee saves little. It saves even less once the free report has already named each key's consumer, which is the hardest part (attribution). The free tier may hand over enough for teams to finish the job themselves, perhaps with AI coding assistants and the clouds' published docs.
legal-ethics

The GitHub permission model is understated and possibly vendor-custodied. The MVP opens PRs that edit .github/workflows files, but it describes the GitHub App as 'org Secrets read and Contents read'. GitHub requires Contents (write) and Workflows (write) to change workflow files, and Pull requests (write) to open PRs. Write access to every repo's CI definitions is a top-tier supply-chain grant. If Keybridge operates one multi-tenant App and holds its private key and webhook endpoint, a vendor breach gives an attacker workflow-write across all customers. That is the round-1 concentration risk in a new form, and it contradicts 'nothing leaves the customer's environment'. Fix: each customer registers its own App (manifest flow) or uses a self-hosted PAT/App, the key stays in the customer's account, and the permissions are stated accurately.

riskiest_assumption.test: Publish the read-only scanner as a script that runs in the customer's account and prints a local report; offer it to 40 platform leads from DevOps communities, the GitHub issues in the evidence and two DevOps consultancies. For those who run it, review the report with them and offer the $6,000 migration with a signed LOI or 50% deposit.
